questions.Section Heading: Application of the cancer clause of section 721 of the act.
questions.Focus: Cancer provision for ingested color additives
questions.Question (ask verbatim): An older study suggests a colorant in our lip product (which may be ingested) caused tumors when fed to rats. How does FDA apply the cancer provision of section 721?
questions.Key Answer Elements: 70.50(a) applies when data suggest the possibility the additive, including components or impurities, induced cancer when ingested (1), or appropriate food-additive tests suggest it (2). On the judgment of appropriately qualified scientists, the Commissioner decides whether cancer was induced and the additive caused it. If not established, the cancer provision does not apply; listing follows if data establish safety. If it induces cancer, no regulation may permit its use.

questions.Section Heading: Application of the cancer clause of section 721 of the act.
questions.Question (ask verbatim): Our skin-only body paint colorant caused tumors in a skin-painting study. What does 70.50 say about external cosmetic use?

questions.Question (ask verbatim): FDA reviewed our petition and won't exempt our new pigment from certification. What does that mean for the listing and for using batches that aren't certified?

questions.Key Answer Elements: 601(c) covers cosmetics 'held' under insanitary conditions, so a holding/distribution site is covered by the adulteration provision. Facilities that only hold/distribute are excluded from the 604 'facility' definition, so no 607 registration. No codified pest-control program rule. Brand as responsible person still bears 605/608 duties.

questions.Question (ask verbatim): A customer emailed that our face mask gave her a rash that went away in a day. Do we have to report it to FDA?
questions.Expected Citation — VERIFIED KEY: FD&C Act 605(a)–(b), (e) (21 U.S.C. 364a); 604 (21 U.S.C. 364) adverse event / serious adverse event
questions.Key Answer Elements: Only serious adverse events must be reported (within 15 business days). A transient rash is an adverse event but not 'serious' unless it meets 604 criteria (e.g., death, hospitalization, infection, significant disfigurement incl. serious and persistent rashes, medical intervention to prevent these). Responsible person must still keep records related to each adverse event report for 6 years (3 years for qualifying small businesses).

questions.Question (ask verbatim): We're a distributor whose name is on the label; the product is made by a contract manufacturer. A user was hospitalized after using our hair-straightening cream. Who reports, by when, and what goes in the report?

questions.Question (ask verbatim): Our contract manufacturer rejected a batch of eye shadow for microbial contamination. Can we rework it, and does any FDA rule govern the reprocessing?
questions.Key Answer Elements: No codified cosmetic reprocessing/rework rule. Distributed product must not be adulterated: 601(b) filthy/putrid/decomposed substance, 601(c) insanitary conditions/injurious to health. 608 requires adequate safety substantiation for the product as marketed. Products that regularly contact the mucous membrane of the eye under customary or usual use are excluded from the 612 small-business exemption from 606/607 (612(b)(1)). No compliance guarantee.
